title: New World
description: Majority of lands of the Western Hemisphere
wiki_lead:
The "New World" (Latin: Mundus novus) is an early modern term describing the majority of lands in the Western Hemisphere, particularly the Americas, and sometimes Oceania. It was introduced in the early 16th century, during Europe's Age of Discovery, by Italian explorer Amerigo Vespucci, who published the pamphlet Mundus novus, presenting his conclusion that the lands discovered west of the Atlantic Ocean (soon called America after Amerigo's name) constituted new continents. 
This realization expanded the geographical horizon of earlier European geographers, who had thought that the world included only Africa, Asia, and Europe, which became collectively known as the "Old World".
wiki_excerpt:
The "New World" (Latin: Mundus novus) is an early modern term describing the majority of lands in the Western Hemisphere, particularly the Americas, and sometimes Oceania. It was introduced in the early 16th century, during Europe's Age of Discovery, by Italian explorer Amerigo Vespucci, who published the pamphlet Mundus novus, presenting his conclusion that the lands discovered west of the Atlantic Ocean (soon called America after Amerigo's name) constituted new continents. 
This realization expanded the geographical horizon of earlier European geographers, who had thought that the world included only Africa, Asia, and Europe, which became collectively known as the "Old World".


Origin of the term

The Florentine explorer Amerigo Vespucci is usually credited for coming up with the term "New World" (Mundus Novus) for the Americas in his 1503 letter, giving it its popular cachet, although similar terms had been used and applied before him.


Prior usage
The Venetian explorer Alvise Cadamosto used the term "un altro mondo" ("another world") to refer to sub-Saharan Africa, which he explored in 1455 and 1456 on behalf of the Portuguese. This was merely a literary flourish, not a suggestion of a new "fourth" part of the world. Cadamosto was aware that sub-Saharan Africa was part of the African continent.
Peter Martyr d'Anghiera, an Italian chronicler at the service of Spain, doubted Christopher Columbus's claims to have reached East Asia ("the Indies"), and consequently came up with alternative names to refer to them. Only a few weeks after Columbus's return from his first voyage, Martyr wrote letters referring to Columbus's discovered lands as the "western antipodes" ("antipodibus occiduis", letter of 14 May 1493), and the "new hemisphere of the earth" ("novo terrarum hemisphaerio", 13 September 1493). 
In a letter dated 1 November 1493, he refers to Columbus as the "discoverer of the new globe" ("Colonus ille novi orbis repertor"). A year later, on 20 October 1494, Peter Martyr again refers to the marvels of the New Globe ("Novo Orbe") and the "Western Hemisphere" ("ab occidente hemisphero").
In Columbus's 1499 letter to the Catholic Monarchs of Spain, reporting the results of his third voyage, he relates how the massive waters of South America's Orinoco delta rushing into the Gulf of Paria implied that a previously unknown continent must lie behind it. Columbus proposes that the South American landmass is not a "fourth" continent, but rather the terrestrial paradise of Biblical tradition, a land allegedly known, but undiscovered, by Christendom. In another letter to the nurse of Prince John, written 1500, Columbus refers to having reached a "new heavens and world" ("nuevo cielo é mundo") and that he had placed "another world" ("otro mundo") under the dominion of the Kings of Spain.

grok_lead: The New World denotes the continents of the Americas âNorth, Central, and Southâencountered by European explorers starting with Christopher Columbus's 1492 voyage to the Caribbean, marking their distinction from the Afro-Eurasian landmass known as the Old World. The term originated in Amerigo Vespucci's 1504 publication Mundus Novus, where he described the lands as a previously unknown fourth continent separate from Asia, based on voyages between 1499 and 1502 that revealed their continental scale and diverse geography. This recognition spurred the Age of Exploration, cartographic advancements like Martin WaldseemÃ¼ller's 1507 map naming "America" after Vespucci, and the integration of the hemispheres into a global system. Central to the New World's historical significance is the Columbian Exchange, the bidirectional transfer of biological and cultural elements post-1492, which reshaped ecosystems and societies worldwide. From the Americas came transformative crops such as maize, potatoes, tomatoes, and tobacco, boosting population growth and caloric intake in the Old World, while Europe introduced wheat, rice, sugar cane, horses, cattle, and pigs, enabling new agricultural and transport paradigms in the Americas. Conversely, Old World pathogens including smallpox, measles, and influenza âagainst which indigenous peoples had no immunityâcaused catastrophic mortality rates, with empirical estimates indicating up to 90% population decline across the Americas by the 17th century, dwarfing direct conflict in scale. These exchanges fostered economic globalization through silver mining in PotosÃ­ and Manila galleon trade but also entrenched inequalities via European colonization, slave labor importation, and resource extraction. Notable achievements include the synthesis of hybrid cultures, technological diffusion like the wheel and ironworking to the Americas, and scientific insights from New World biodiversity challenging Old World paradigms. Controversies persist over interpretive biases in academic narratives, which often emphasize colonial exploitation while understating indigenous agency and pre-contact advancements in agriculture, urbanism, and astronomy among civilizations like the Maya, Inca, and Mississippian cultures; causal analysis prioritizes epidemiological and ecological factors over ideological framings. The New World's legacy endures in modern demographics, cuisines, and hemispheric interdependencies.
